The two figures are reported separately and are never averaged. Quarantine downtime means opposite things for the two groups: an isolated attacker is zero-trust enforcement working, an isolated honest node is the system’s real cost. A single fleet-wide "availability: 94%" would be a mean over two quantities that should move in opposite directions.

Attack impact — on vs. off

The same metrics before and after the first timed attack armed at 15s — measured impact, not a detection flag. Onsets: iot38 spoof @15s, srv3 sybil @20s, srv6 drop @30s, srv1 grayhole @40s, srv8 onoff @50s, iot37 flood @60s.

Read this table with care: the clean window is run start-up, not a clean steady state. The first timed attack arms at 15s, and the clean window is only 1 bucket wide; honest trust is still climbing through it (0.62 to 0.62, against 0.81 later) — it has not reached steady state; no VIP flow rule had been installed yet, so measured throughput is zero for reasons that have nothing to do with the attack. Several rows below therefore show the attack window looking better — that is the run warming up, not the attack helping. The numbers are left as measured rather than trimmed to a flattering window; to get a real baseline, arm the first attack later so a steady-state clean window exists.

The online UCB1 bandit is a separate mechanism and is live on the dashboard.

Both losses are in the clean scenario, with no attacker present, and the cause is not the trust term. Every load-reactive strategy reads a load view that refreshes once per poll while tasks finish in ~0.2 s, so each arrival inside a polling window is routed on the same stale snapshot and herds onto whichever node last looked idle. Sweeping the poll interval separates this exactly: the two load-blind strategies are flat at every poll (they never read the signal), everything that does read it improves monotonically as the signal gets fresher, and by a 0.01 s poll zt_sdn is the best strategy on the board. The clean-case cost is a tuning property of the 1 s poll, not a property of trust-aware routing. Full sweep in docs/EVALUATION.md §6.

Read the latency column against the failure column. A router that loses tasks to a black hole never measures them: they time out, they are counted as failures, and they never enter the latency average. So a strategy can post a competitive p95 precisely because its worst tasks are missing from it. Latency alone is not a safe metric under a drop attack, which is why SLO violation rate — where a task that never completed counts as a violation — is the primary metric on this page.
